As the story of a soccer team gone cannibal kicks off in 1996, Yellowjackets has plumbed the depths of '90s music to make one banger soundtrack season after season. This year, if you're looking to play (or headbang) along, we've got you covered with the needle drops of Season 4 as each episode hits.

Sources indicate that but that's not all. Sure, you can use this collection to built a killer playlist. (Buzz, buzz!) We're also going to dive into a bit of what it means and why each song might have been selected for its particular Yellowjackets moment.

Let's kick things off with the Season 4 premiere:.

Sample lyric: If I could find that Heina / And that Sancho that she's found / Well, I'd pop a cap in Sancho / And I'd slap her down.

Season 4 opens with this hit song that had a total chokehold on teens in 1996. The lyrics sing of a hapless dude making messy decisions.

Fittingly, it plays while teen Jeff (Jack DePew) is getting high on the job at Taylor's Furniture Store with his doofy bestie Randy (Riley Baron). Despite some violent lyrics, "Santeria" is a upbeat tune that speaks to Jeff's laid-back attitude, post-graduation.

But once he sees the news of the Yellowjackets rescue on TV, the theme song cuts in and dramatically changes the episode's tone.

Sample lyric: It was cool / Nothing fire / Nothing broke / Keep simple / Nothing tired / Nothing old / Same as you / Same as you.

For four seasons now, this song's cryptic lyrics have played as a pitch-perfect distillation of the show's female rage, rooted in lust, jealousy, and even love.

Sample lyric: My girl, my girl, don't lie to me / Tell me, where did you sleep last night?In the pines, in the pines / Where the sun don't ever shine / I would shiver the whole night through.

After the opening credits, Yellowjackets picks up with the titular team in a hospital, where they are safe but look worried, likely about the world learning how it is they made it through their ordeal.

Playing over the sequence is Kurt Cobain's cover of the American folk song also known as "In the Pines," which is recognized as a murder ballad. The lyrics reflect a haunting story of homicide in the woods. The particular song has been covered by a variety of acts since its creation in the 1870s, including the father of Bluegrass Bill Monroe, Blues singer Lead Belly, and Dolly Parton.

It has been revealed that cobain famously covered the song on his MTV Unplugged appearance, on Nov. 18, 1993. So, it's a cover the Yellowjackets themselves might recognize. Moreover, his grunge rendition reflects the trauma and terror of the team's return to civilization.

Sample lyric: For the life of me, I cannot remember / What made us think that we were wise and we'd never compromise / For the life of me, I cannot believe / We'd ever die for these sins, we were merely freshmen.

This '90s song plays in the present timeline, but in a meaningful way. Showing up to Shauna's (Melanie Lynskey) door in episode 1, Melissa (Hilary Swank) presents a bottle of wine along with the news that she's moved in next door, and that she's called the press. Shauna looks on in shock asking, "What did you do?" as "The Freshmen" plays.

From 1997, this hit song from the Verve Pipe tells the tale of two young men, reflecting on the damage they've done to a shared lover. In this context, "The Freshmen" plays as if Shauna's subconscious is making an excuse ("we were merely freshmen").

It has been revealed that or perhaps, this song's use use here is meant to reflect Melissa's perspective. As the wounded lover, her story could show what might happen if that lover struck back with the poetic justice of reclaiming her narrative and her future.

  • In a recent development, microsoft is shutting down its To Do app at the end of June 2027, with focus moving to the newer Planner app.
  • According to recent reports, as we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft confirmed this week that its To Do app is shutting down soon, taking the legacy of Wunderlist with it.

In a recent development, microsoft is shutting down its To Do app at the end of June 2027, with focus moving to the newer Planner app. The company explains:.

According to recent reports, as we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do. The To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027. Connections that other apps use to access To Do tasks will continue beyond that date, and we’ll provide separate notice before those connections are retired. We’re also updating existing task integrations across Microsoft 365 to connect with Planner, so you’ll be able to create or manage tasks in the Microsoft experiences you already use. Although To Do tasks are already visible in Planner, they will not be migrated to the upcoming private initiative. Customers using personal Microsoft accounts will need to choose another app. Our To Do transition guidance  will help you understand what’s changing and plan your next steps.

To Do was built on the foundation of Wunderlist, a wildly popular to do list app that Microsoft purchased in 2015. Wunderlist later shut down in 2020.

Microsoft’s shuffle, notably, leaves general consumers without a replacement app. To Do was available to anyone with a Microsoft account, where Planner is available only to enterprise/business users. So, for long-time Wunderlist users who followed Microsoft migration, this is the end of the road and it’s officially time to move to another app.

If you're looking for a tablet and have a budget of just £100, then your options are usually extremely limited: entry-level models like the Lenovo Tab One or the Samsung Galaxy Tab A11 often go for more than £150.

According to recent reports, luckily, Amazon has come to the rescue with its brand-new Alexa Tablet line, which has seen a huge swathe of discounts in the ongoing early Black Friday sales. According to recent reports, although the specs are modest, you're still getting a fully functional, working tablet for under £100, and in 2026 that's worth shouting about. In Season 4, Episode 1, here are all the curious images we noticed:.

It has been revealed that melanie Lynskey is shown wide-mouthed before a microphone, suggesting adult Shauna has something to say (or sing?) in Season 4. Considering Shauna has a special skill for brutal one-liners, whoever she's looking at should be trembling.

Under blood and a prosthetic broken nose, Sophie Nélisse is hard to recognize in the moment. But freeze-frame the credits, and there's no doubt that's Teen Shauna. She's lying in the snow. So, presumably this is still when the girls were in the wilderness.

At the end of the Season 3, Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) successfully reached the outside world through the frog scientist's SAT phone. So, what happens before rescue comes?

The colors of this shot are brighter and more saturated than Yellowjackets tends to go. The uniform is a throwback 1950s style, and actress Tawny Cypress is smiling in a wide-eyed way that's not in keeping with Taissa's character. So, we're speculating this will be another dream sequence or vision. This one feel Lynchian, and as his work touches on doomed romances and the dark underbelly of suburbia, one can assume he'd speak to Taissa on both levels. But what does it mean?

Her face is covered by a mask, but there's no mistaking her frizzy blond hair and glasses. Will the girls' return to civilization show Misty's path to working at the old folks home? Or will this be a dream sequence where she imagines what her future might be?

In the credits, it's a close-up of what appears to be Shauna, wearing a blindfold and holding a string. To get a fuller context, you have to look to the sneak peek images Paramount released on Nov. 5.

There you can see a wider shot:.

Here you can see she's holding a knife on a string while standing inside the crashed plane, her team huddled on the floor around her. This recalls the ritual seance the girls did in Season 1 in the cabin's attic. They'd tried to contact the presumed dead owner of the cabin, and instead tapped into something darker and more mysterious.

The swinging knife is meant to answer the girls' questions. So, are they calling on the "it" of the wilderness for advice ahead of their rescue?

Whose head is being pried open in this nightmarish way? It's hard to tell from the close-up, which gives away no facial features. Dark hair and a sleeve ending in lace are the only clues. But based on the outrageousness, we're going to guess this one is a nightmare within the show.

This set dressing was spotted by fans on Reddit eight months back. But what's its role in the show? Well, we know Jackie's parents have money. Could this be how they memorialize their golden girl?

That's probably bad news for Shauna, right?

Christina Ricci's been a violent ax-wielder before. (We remember Lizzie Borden Took an Ax and The Lizzie Borden Chronicles). We also know an ax is how Edwin died last season — though by Lottie's hand. Yet despite Misty's maniacal facial expression, and her still wearing Natalie's leather jacket, we're guess this is more a Misty-to-the-rescue moment. Maybe she's about to pull a Shining and ax a door?

Where is she? WHO IS SHE AIMING AT?

As this is shot comes from the opening scene of Season 4, there's not much mystery here. Teen Jeff (Jack DePew) had moved on from Shauna and Jackie, getting high with Randy (Riley Baron) and working at Jackie's parents' furniture story. Then he sees her face on the news, with reports of their rescue.

With Shauna finally coming back from the wilderness, we're likely to see how grief and love brought these two together for a marriage we may not envy, but kind of admire?

Valve says it might have to raise the price of supply-limited Steam Machines

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (439 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when the Steam Machine first started shipping in June, Valve mentioned it was producing fewer units at a higher price than initially planned because it couldn’t secure supplies of scarce RAM and storage components at a reasonable cost.
  • According to recent reports, “We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels,” Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday.
  • If Valve does have to raise the price of the Steam Machine, it will be in good organization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when the Steam Machine first started shipping in June, Valve mentioned it was producing fewer units at a higher price than initially planned because it couldn’t secure supplies of scarce RAM and storage components at a reasonable cost. Now, as the last of the initial batch of Steam Machine reservations are finally being fulfilled, Valve says those supply and cost concerns will continue into the foreseeable future and may even require a price change.

According to recent reports, “We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels,” Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday. “As a result we don’t yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we’ll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained.”.

If Valve does have to raise the price of the Steam Machine, it will be in good organization. All three major console manufacturers instituted historically atypical price increases in 2025, with additional price hikes happening this year.

For the Steam Machine, though, Valve may be more susceptible to supply-related price shocks than its larger competitors in the gaming hardware space. Valve “likely [doesn’t] have the same kind of priority as a Nintendo, Sony, or Microsoft when it comes to suppliers,” F-Squared analyst Michael Futter told us earlier this year. And while the bigger players can still negotiate somewhat with chip suppliers, Valve’s Steam Machine is “a niche product that cannot benefit in the same way when it comes to procurement,” Niko Partners analyst Daniel Ahmad noted.

It has been revealed that while Valve has not publicly discussed total Steam Machine sales, estimates based on public Steam Top Sellers charts suggest the company was selling 12,000 to 15,000 a week back in July. By contrast, the PS5 has averaged over 300,000 weekly unit sales worldwide in its roughly six years on the market.

Sources indicate that for now, at least, Valve notes it has fulfilled an expectation it set in July that “everyone in the reservation queue will have the option to purchase by the end of this year.” The company now says there is “no waitlist remaining” for the 512GB Steam Machine model and that “purchase invites” have been sent to the remaining randomized 2TB reservation holders (who placed orders back in April). The 512GB model was even briefly back in stock on the Steam Store yesterday, even as Valve continues to pare down the waitlist for 2TB stock.

Valve says it plans to release additional updates on Steam Machine availability in January.

So the cost of the overall device is more influenced by memory prices than in a flagship, like the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Even with a specced-out build, there’s more dispersion of costly components, rather than one expensive component like memory taking up the bulk of the production price.

That cut is estimated to be around 10 million units, and this latest report only furthers the claim that mid-range devices are too costly to make for Samsung.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smartphones and social media have completely changed the way youngsters communicate and interact with each other, but one tech organization wants to resurrect a classic method of communication so kids can chat with each other just like the good old days.

Seattle-based brand Tin Can has been reinventing the landline phone for the younger generation for the past two years, and now the kid-friendly mobile devices are finally making their UK debut on November 30, mimicking the design and feel of landline devices that are now a thing of the past. But these aren't fake Fisher-Price toys — these things actually work.

In a recent development, vibrant and bold in design, Tin Can phones are wired to ensure your child has access to a safer means of communication. Each Tin Can device is Wi-Fi enabled, deliberately leaving screens and algorithms behind for a basic, simplified experience. Yes, shielding young customers from the dangers of digital malice in the age of social media is important, but the brains behind the Tin Can brand want to promote real conversations and independence for its young users. #1814. Army delays detonating "catastrophically hazardous" lead azide amid fear, anger

Army delays detonating "catastrophically hazardous" lead azide amid fear, anger

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1389 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army unveiled Thursday that it would delay a blueprint to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air.
  • In a recent development, the Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs).
  • In a recent development, “Public communication is essential to public trust,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle stated in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army unveiled Thursday that it would delay a blueprint to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. A federal appeals court further halted plans later on Thursday with an emergency order. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week.

In a recent development, the Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). Prior to the court stay, the Army rescheduled the blast until November 23 to provide more time to communicate about the situation with Iowans, who have reported being unaware of the detonations until earlier this week.

In a recent development, “Public communication is essential to public trust,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle stated in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday. “Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information.”.

Industry observers note that telle claimed that the Army could not delay the detonation any further than Monday due to the state of deterioration of the compound, which is extremely explosive and sensitive. “This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”.

In a recent development, lead azide is a compound used in detonators for munitions and is stockpiled by the US military. In March, the US Army identified that the stockpile in the Iowa facility—the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP)—had deteriorated. The lead azide in the 68 barrels, reported to total around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons), is suspended in a mixture of water and ethanol within the ECMs, but has degraded and crystallized over time. Temperature fluctuations can cause lead azide to dissolve into the water/alcohol solution and recrystallize into needles or platelets, the Army said. In crystallized forms, lead azide becomes extremely sensitive to any physical shock, friction, or heat. The Army determined the current state is a “catastrophically hazardous condition.”.

Recent findings suggest that in an environmental assessment released Wednesday, the Army noted that trying to move the lead azide from its current position for any reason was ruled out. Any sloshing or physical shock from loading, transporting, or burying the barrels for safer detonation would create “an unacceptable safety risk and a high probability of accidental, uncontrolled detonation.”.

The military considered neutralizing the lead azide using a chemical reagent, but again ruled it out because it said the process would require handling the lead azide over an extended period, with barrels neutralized at a rate of 3 to 10 per day. “The chemical neutralization process requires significantly more ‘hands-on’ time and physical manipulation of the drums by personnel over a prolonged 7- to 22-day period, drastically increasing the probability of accidental, fatal detonation during handling,” the Army wrote in its assessment.

In all, the Army considered a controlled, mitigated “Blow-in-Place” proposal the best option, and it specifically planned for a fall detonation. The Army said the fall weather would “take advantage of periods of reduced thermal cycling and to ensure the lowest impact to facility operations and local agriculture (harvesting).”.

According to an emergency permit for the detonation from the Environmental Protection Agency, the strategy is to place explosive charges and an accelerant on or near each of the ECMs.

The Army intends to try to mitigate the detonation’s impact with a few simple methods. Those include lime-fill and sand-fill barriers around the ECMs, water cannons and misters to control lead dust in the wake of the explosion, and timing the detonation with ideal weather conditions—avoiding high winds that could increase the area exposed to the plume or, conversely, a thermal inversion that could trap the plume in one place.

Modeling released Wednesday—based on the conditions for the scheduled detonation on Friday—suggested the plume could deposit lead dust at an amount between 5 and 100 micrograms per square foot in a stretch up to 25 miles north, nearly to Wapello, Iowa. Those levels are above those considered hazardous for floors and windows, respectively. Meanwhile, airborne lead, at a level of 0.18 micrograms per cubic meter, would reach nearly 100 miles north, toward Cedar Rapids, Iowa. The EPA standard for lead levels in the air is 0.15 micrograms per cubic meter.

In a recent development, during the detonation, the Army advised residents in the immediate area to consider leaving or at least staying indoors with windows closed. It also recommended people wash their cars if they park outside. Similarly, local fire departments reportedly planned to hose down children’s playgrounds to remove any coating of lead dust in the aftermath, and schools planned closures.

The Army’s plan was to communicate clearly with the public about the aims, including holding an open-house event on October 15. But while Middletown residents may have been aware of the detonations, Iowans in the projected path of the plume were surprised by the news this week.

Recent findings suggest that in its environmental risk assessment, the Army remarked it planned to mitigate the lead fallout with “rapid excavation” of soil and dust and treat it with a “stabilization agent.” This was to prevent it from remaining in the environment of the military facility, from which it could drift or make its way into groundwater. But the efforts would not mitigate the airborne plume, and lead does not break down in the environment. Children and pregnant people are particularly vulnerable to the neurotoxic effects.

Amid health and environmental fears, state leaders and residents raised a range of questions Wednesday and Thursday, from how the lead azide was allowed to deteriorate to its current hazardous condition and whether the Army had truly exhausted safer options—options that wouldn’t launch a toxic cloud over a swath of the state.

Iowa’s governor-elect, Rob Sand, wrote on social media that an “unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation.”.

Political leaders in nearby Illinois also chimed in, sending a letter to Telle and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, expressing “grave concerns” over the initiative.

“Alongside our neighbors in Iowa, we are also demanding answers about how this could affect our people’s health and safety,” Illinois Governor JB Pritzker wrote on social media.

Recent findings suggest that on Thursday, prior to the announcement of a delay, environmental groups filed a lawsuit seeking a court-ordered pause of the detonation. The groups alleged, in part, that the EPA approved the proposal “without full consideration of less dangerous alternatives that would avoid widespread dispersal and deposition of toxic lead; and inadequate public notice of the plan to open-detonate hazardous waste due to the extraordinarily rushed timeline set by the Army.” Late Thursday, a federal appeals court issued an emergency stay of the Army’s EPA permit for the demolition, halting intends until it can review the case.

Friday morning, the Army, Department of Health and Human Services, and EPA released a joint statement saying:.

Industry observers note that the entire interagency is working together to ensure that the controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa is conducted in the safest fashion possible. Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized. The entire Trump administration will continue to engage with state and local officials, as well as the broader community, to keep all apprised of updates as they arise.

Notably, in June, Zeldin listed the EPA’s work with Iowa’s lead azide as one of the top “100 environmental victories that showcase EPA’s unwavering dedication to protecting American families.” The work was number 60 on the list, described as providing “critical emergency support to Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, deploying technical experts for 68 deteriorating drums of explosive lead azide.”.

This post was updated November 20 to include that the federal appeals court granted a stay in the case brought by the environmental groups.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

Snapchat has 3 latest ways to help creators get discovered

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (864 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A creator's video can put a restaurant on someone's weekend list, send shoppers looking for a product, or make a brand want to work with the person who posted it.
  • 18, Snap declared three updates that make it easier for 1) followers to find places their favorite creators recommend, 2) brands to find creators to work with, and 3) agencies to run those campaigns.
  • Here's how each revision works and how Snapchat's approach compares with what other social platforms are already doing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A creator's video can put a restaurant on someone's weekend list, send shoppers looking for a product, or make a brand want to work with the person who posted it. Snapchat wants to integrate more of that routine into Snapchat.

On Nov. 18, Snap declared three updates that make it easier for 1) followers to find places their favorite creators recommend, 2) brands to find creators to work with, and 3) agencies to run those campaigns. If you're a creator, that could mean more ways to make money from the videos you already post and another place for people to find your recommendations.

Here's how each revision works and how Snapchat's approach compares with what other social platforms are already doing.

In a recent development, snap Map already works a little like a neighborhood guide. For example, if you tap on a bakery, there's a listing with its hours, directions, and reviews. Now, with a feature called Visited By, Snapchat can also show that a creator you follow has been there and give you a link to their post.

Here's how it works. Using the same bakery example — if a food creator reviews a bakery and tags it in a public post on Spotlight, Snapchat's short-video feed, or posts the review directly to Snap Map with the same tag. Snapchat can then highlight the store on the map for that creator's followers. So if you missed the video when it first went up, you could still come across it while looking for pastry, watch a creator's review, and send the spot to a friend in Chat. The feature is available globally, and Snap notes more than 450 million people use Snap Map each month.

Snap states people already share creators' recommendations in Chat when they're talking about "where to go next or what to buy." Visited By gives them a new way to share a business. Snap also sees the sharing part as a way for creators to reach people who don't already follow them.

"For creators, it means more visibility for the places and experiences they share, helping them connect with their existing followers and build new ones as their recommendations are shared with friends," the organization wrote.

Industry observers note that this announcement comes a few weeks after TikTok gave its own users an in-app way to go from watching a restaurant video to booking a table. In October, it released Must Eat, a dining guide built from videos, reviews, and comments across the app.

Recent findings suggest that snapchat is also changing how advertisers find creators to work with. The revamped Snap Creator Network, now in open beta, lets a brand describe the audience it wants to reach, the type of content it needs, or what it hopes the campaign will accomplish. Snap uses AI to suggest creators, and brands can then review how their content performs, save a shortlist, message creators about a partnership, or pay to promote a post they've already made.

"Our aim is to make creator discovery and outreach more efficient, while maintaining the creator's voice within their own communities," Snap wrote in the blog post. "For creators, this means greater opportunities to work with some of their favorite brands and be discovered for the right audience fit, not just follower count.".

Eligible creators can opt in by turning on Brand Partnerships in their Public Profile settings. That lets approved brands reach out directly on Snapchat to work together or to use a video the creator has already posted in an ad.

Sometimes the team reaching out to a creator is an agency working on the brand's behalf. Snap is giving those teams more help, too, through its expanded Creator Agency Partner Program. The program, according to Snap, equips "agencies with the training, support, and incentive access they need to build and scale Creator Ads on Snapchat.".

According to recent reports, other social platforms have similar pipelines in place: TikTok One matches advertisers with creators based on a campaign brief, lets brands promote approved posts as Spark Ads, and gives agencies tools to manage contracts and track campaigns. Meta's Creator Marketing Hub, on the other hand, brings creator search, outreach, and Partnership Ads together across Instagram and Facebook.

There's a reason Snap, TikTok, and Meta are all making it easier for brands to find creators and turn their posts into ads. The Interactive Advertising Bureau projected that U.S. creator ad spending would reach $44 billion in 2026, and brands in its research noted finding the right creator was their biggest challenge. The easier a platform makes it to find someone, reach out, and run an ad, the better its shot at a slice of that (pretty large) pie.

The latest quarterly data for the US smartphone market reveals that Google Pixel is holding its ground despite the overall market faltering, and the other two major Android brands struggling.

Recent findings suggest that the top smartphone brands in the United States include Apple, Samsung, Motorola, and Google Pixel in that order. Apple continues to absolutely dominate at a whopping 57% market share in Q3 2026, up from 50% during the same period last year.

Samsung came in at 25%, up 1% from last year (likely driven by a very successful Fold 8 launch during Q3), while Motorola shrank from 12% to 8%.

Sources indicate that google Pixel made up 6%, down 1% from Q3 2025, Counterpoint Research highlights. Q3 is notable for Google as it includes the company’s new August release window for new flagships. It’s not surprising that Google dropped a percentage point year-over-year, as the company’s Pixel 11 launch was not particularly exciting, especially as prices rose over the previous generation. If anything, only dropping 1% must be pretty encouraging given the overall market conditions and RAMageddon of it all.

Something to note – Google Pixel is technically growing this year compared to last. Just out of view on this latest upgrade, Q2 2026 saw Google’s share up 1% year-over-year, and Q1 was also up compared to the same period in 2025. Counterpoint previously mentioned that the Pixel brand “remains aggressive in postpaid” carriers, but notes that Pixel 11 shipments were “weaker YoY.”.

Apple’s ‘just works’ approach is great, but goes a little too far

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (945 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that “It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple.
  • Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….
  • Macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that “It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple. Interestingly, it appears to have been coined by the organization’s customers and then used by reviewers before it was later picked up by Steve Jobs.

Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….

Macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing. It was subsequently used by a number of reviewers. The earliest example I can find of Steve Jobs adopting it was in 1999, when discussing the rollout of FireWire to the Mac in the PowerMac G3.

It’s hot-pluggable. You don’t have to turn your computer off to connect and disconnect peripherals, you can just plug them right in. Again, the drivers are dynamically loaded. There are no terminators and there are no switches. It just works.

(If you have a link to any earlier example, please do let me know in the comments.).

I’m a substantial fan of the philosophy. Most of the time, people should just be able to get on with the tasks they want to execute without having to worry about the technology. The tech that makes it all possible should sit there quietly in the background.

However, there are cases where I think Apple takes this approach a little too far, and where tech-savvy users at least would like a little more transparency and control.

AirPods firmware updates are a good example. Back in September, there was quite a significant enhancement in the form of custom EQ. It’s a rather basic version, but still a feature many had wanted for a long time. Instead of being able to manually trigger the update, customers had to wait until it “just worked.”.

Industry observers note that apple’s support document has a how-to guide that is essentially an outline of the conditions required to permit an update, and an instruction to simply wait until it happens. Which you will only know by repeatedly checking.

Make sure your AirPods are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Connect your charging case to a power source. Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid. Keep the lid of the charging case closed, and keep your AirPods in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to be updated. Check the firmware version again.

Another example, and one I’ve complained about before, is that there is no way to manually trigger an iCloud document sync, nor any progress indicator when it does finally happen. In the best of cases, it takes seconds; in the worst, many hours. And again, the only way to find out is to repeatedly check.

Recent findings suggest that it’s the same story when shooting a video on your iPhone. Will it still be there an hour later, available to instantly edit and view? Maybe, or maybe it will have been offloaded to the cloud, requiring it to be downloaded before you can do anything with it – while a video you shot months earlier is still stored locally on the device! You can, of course, switch off optimization altogether, but if you choose to use it, you get no control over it. I want a setting that allows me to do things like specify local retention of all photos and videos taken within the past fortnight.

Will that video be available in the Mac Photos app when you check half an hour later? Maybe, maybe not. You can click the Sync Now button as many times as you like, and it will apparently have no effect, claiming it’s up to date despite the video being entirely absent. It will be there when it’s there.

Recent findings suggest that once it is in the Photos app on your Mac, it’s a similar story when exporting it to a folder. You can drag and drop the video into the folder, and this time you are manually triggering the transfer (yay!), but there will be absolutely no visual indication that it is in progress. No grayed-out icon, no progress bar, nothing. So far as the user interface is concerned, it appears that your drag and drop had no effect – until the video file finally appears.

According to recent reports, I think with all of these things and more, Apple needs to offer options. Yes, most non-tech customers may be perfectly happy to just wait until things happen, but there ought to be a standard way to trigger things that currently happen in their own sweet time, as well as progress indicators and confirmation that a process is complete.

Industry observers note that is this an ecosystem-wide improvement you’d like to see? Please share your thoughts in the comments and add any frustrating examples of your own.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week I reported that Huawei was set to launch a new sub-brand called OSTA, with its first phone being an interesting wide-screen model called the OSTA O1 Pro. As of today, everything has been made official — and the OSTA O1 Pro is available to order now via the Huawei VMALL site in China.

According to recent reports, as reliable Weibo tipsters suggested, the OSTA O1 Pro does indeed boast a unique wide form factor. Thanks to a newly uploaded spec sheet, we now know that it has a 6.39-inch display with a 120Hz refresh rate, starts at 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, and is powered by the Kirin 9030S chipset – the same mid-range chip as the standard Huawei Pura 90.

According to recent reports, the phone has a 7,000mAh battery, with support for 66W SuperCharge and 5W wired reverse charging, as well as 50W wireless charging when using a compatible charger. As for the cameras, the OSTA O1 Pro has a 200MP main shooter paired with a 50MP telephoto lens. There doesn't seem to be a dedicated ultra-wide or macro lens present. There is, however, a 50MP selfie camera on the front of the phone.

Industry observers note that the OSTA O1 Pro is available in three colours: Starry Night Black, Nebula White, and Starlight Purple (though the latter is only offered in 16GB+512GB and 16GB+1TB configurations). Prices start at 5699 CNY for the most basic model, which comes to roughly $855 or £650.

It has been revealed that the OSTA O1 Pro would be a pretty unexceptional mid-range phone, were it not for that unique wide-screen format. It almost looks like an iPhone Air, but fatter and more... compressed. That's not a bad thing either, as I think wider formats like this definitely have a place.

The popularity of the Samsung Galaxy Fold 8 (which is similarly stout) highlights that Android people are certainly interested in trying form factors that are a bit more out there than the usual candy bar shape. The design of the OSTA O1 Pro also just looks like it would be very comfortable in the hands and fit comfortably in most pockets.

Wider aspect ratios have advantages when it comes to multitasking too, as they make it easier to view multiple windows side by side when using the phone horizontally.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

According to recent reports, the major question is whether the OSTA O1 Pro will make it to the West in any official capacity and, sadly, I don't think it's likely. Huawei pulled out of the US market following a US government ban in 2022 and has largely stopped selling its handsets in the UK as well. The only phones currently listed on the Huawei UK site are the Mate XT Ultimate Design and Mate X6 foldable, neither of which is actually available to buy on the store.

That mentioned, we might still see other manufacturers come out with their own wide-screen model – especially if the OSTA O1 Pro proves popular with Chinese consumers.

GTA 6: How to listen to the radio outside of a vehicle

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the most vital aspects of any Grand Theft Auto game is the soundtrack, and for the first time in the series, GTA 6 doesn't require players to be in a car or near a radio to listen to it.
  • Recent findings suggest that rockstar Games went above and beyond licensing dozens of existing bangers across almost any genre you can imagine for GTA 6's in-game radio stations, and that's before you even get to the fantastic original score from Justice.
  • Thankfully, Rockstar Games took a cue from how people listen to music in 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most vital aspects of any Grand Theft Auto game is the soundtrack, and for the first time in the series, GTA 6 doesn't require players to be in a car or near a radio to listen to it.

Recent findings suggest that rockstar Games went above and beyond licensing dozens of existing bangers across almost any genre you can imagine for GTA 6's in-game radio stations, and that's before you even get to the fantastic original score from Justice. However, one small limitation of previous games in the series was that you couldn't really enjoy all of that music while walking around.

Thankfully, Rockstar Games took a cue from how people listen to music in 2026. Here is how to listen to music in GTA 6 without driving a car.

In a recent development, in real life, most people have a pair of headphones or earbuds handy so they can listen to music on their phones. GTA 6 joins some other open-world action games like Watch Dogs 2 in allowing players to use virtual headphones to jam out to some tunes from a smart device while simply walking around the world. The best part is that you can do this from a very early point in the game, though it will require a little bit of in-game money.

According to recent reports, protagonist Jason Duval is perhaps the only guy in Leonida who doesn't own headphones of any kind at the start of GTA 6, so you'll have to go buy some. This can be done at any electronics store in Vice City and the surrounding areas, and you'll know a store sells headphones if the store's icon on the in-game map is a pair of headphones. Convenient!

Recent findings suggest that unless you really branch out right away and decide to explore the whole map before getting on with the story, the easiest way to get headphones at the start is to drive up north from Jason's neighborhood to the town of Hamlet. Some of the early main story missions will take you there, anyway. What you're looking for is a store called Zeke's Electronics on the north side of Hamlet.

Simply go in and you'll be able to buy either over-ear headphones or earbuds next to the cash register. Over-ear cans will run you about $200, while earbuds cost $119. I can't tell if there's a meaningful difference between the two aside from looks, so just go with whatever you like more.

Once you have your headphones, simply hold left on the D-pad to listen to the radio while outside of a car. I recommend the Dirty South Classics station, personally, but your mileage may vary. #1808. Boys Noize turns to the club (and an obscure Italian synth) for inspiration on 7LLVSION

Boys Noize turns to the club (and an obscure Italian synth) for inspiration on 7LLVSION

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (570 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re wondering how Alex Ridha’s (aka Boys Noize) collaboration with Nine Inch Nails influenced his new record 7LLVSION, the answer is simple: It didn’t.
  • Sources indicate that “I do the same I kind of always do.
  • On 7LLVSION, Ridha frequently turned to an obscure Italian semimodular synth, the Grp A4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

‘I always look for the newest machines.’.

If you’re wondering how Alex Ridha’s (aka Boys Noize) collaboration with Nine Inch Nails influenced his new record 7LLVSION, the answer is simple: It didn’t. That’s not to say Ridha didn’t learn anything from the virtuosic production team of Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, but most of the songs on 7LLVSION had been knocking around for some time. And as Ridha is quick to point out, these are not rock songs built for live performance; they’re “battle tested” for clubs and DJ sets. “I was kind of back on the usual kind of thing,” he tells The Verge.

Sources indicate that “I do the same I kind of always do. I go make coffee, go in my room, put on the machines, and I’ll start messing around with sounds and build one sound to another and there comes a record,” he notes. Like previous Boys Noize releases, a lot of 7LLVSION starts with sound design. “It’s kind of tech-driven, in a way,” he says, “because I always look for the newest machines.”.

On 7LLVSION, Ridha frequently turned to an obscure Italian semimodular synth, the Grp A4. “It’s just so powerful, and it sounds so significant,” he claims. The routing options, dual filters (which he uses in parallel), and built-in sequencer kept leading him to new and inspiring places. Because of that, the A4 ended up on a number of tracks, including “Shut It Down,” “1+1+1,” and “Ycore.”.

“The exciting part is always to, you know, not repeat myself, even with the drum sounds, and try something fresh that I haven’t tried before,” Ridha says. For a few tracks, that meant getting away from the rigid, quantized grooves of techno and opting for a more dynamic, live feeling on tracks like “Shut It Down” and “1+1+1” especially. “Live drums are the new 808,” he says.

It has been revealed that he looked to German bands of the ’70s and ’80s for inspiration, like Can, Amon Düül, and Deutsch Amerikanische Freundschaft. He also called out Conny Plank, who produced landmark records by Neu!, Kraftwerk, and Eurythmics. But in general he says, “My goal is to not sound like anything you can point to. You know, I don’t want to be a direct copy.” Instead, he was chasing the sound of “electronic punk.” That means aggressive basslines, driving drums, and stripped-down arrangements that avoid overstuffing the mix with too many instruments.

But it all comes back to the club at the end of the day. “Environment has always been the main thing in my music. I need to have a record that I want to play at the party,” he states, and that meant testing the songs off 7LLVSION extensively in his DJ sets and letting the audience tell him what works and what doesn’t. “The club is the most open and objective situation you can have,” he says. “They don’t know what I’m playing, so they hear something for the first time, and you can just look at someone’s face, or someone’s there in the room to get a cool reaction, and that usually makes me feel good about something or not.”.

Boys Noize is currently touring the world on the festival circuit, and 7LLVSION is available now on most major streaming services.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Garmin and Bark are competing for your money this year, and these sales make it easy to get something fun that’ll keep your kids safe and in touch.

Many parents struggle with the idea of getting a smartphone for their kids. If you want your kids to stay in touch but not have access to all the garbage on the internet, a smartwatch is the best alternative. I’ve tested a lot of kids’ smartwatches over the years, and I can easily recommend the two in the picture above: the Bark Watch and the Garmin Bounce 2.

Both watches are on sale well ahead of Black Friday, too! The Bark Watch is $11 off at Amazon ($274 total) and $50 off at Bark, while the Garmin Bounce 2 is $50-$64 off (starting at $235) depending on the color you choose. The least expensive Garmin Bounce 2 is the blue color in the photo I took above, which my son loved.

Industry observers note that choosing between the two is easy enough. Garmin’s watch is the least complicated and comes in a slightly more durable case with fun colors. It’s slightly cheaper than Bark, but doesn’t have any health sensors on board. It mainly tracks steps, allows your kids to message or call you, and gives you geofencing and location tracking through a $9.99 per month LTE subscription plan. It’s got a 5ATM rating and a polycarbonate case, so it’s quite durable.

It has been revealed that the Garmin Bounce 2 is preloaded with a few mini games and educational apps, plus the Garmin Jr. app has built-in unlockables and rewards parents can set for doing chores, completing schoolwork, etc. Battery life is roughly 2 days with normal use, but can be less if you’re in an area with poor LTE reception. The Garmin Bounce 2 is best for kids 10 and under.

Recent findings suggest that the Bark Watch uses Samsung Galaxy Watch 8 hardware and a custom version of Wear OS. It’s a much more powerful watch and only gets a day of battery life because of it. This one feels like a midpoint between a kids’ watch and a standard Wear OS watch, as it has all the power of Wear OS but doesn’t feature the Google Play Store. It doesn’t have any games, social media, or browsers.

Sources indicate that since it uses Samsung’s hardware, it includes cutting-edge health sensors that your kids can use, plus great multitasking and a svelte, attractive design. Bark charges $15 per month for its blueprint, which includes a Bark App subscription for the whole family. I also use the Bark App on my son’s phone, which helps me monitor his usage and make sure he’s safe online. The extra $5 per month adds up, but it’s absolutely worth it if you want to add the Bark App to another phone or tablet.

The Bark Watch is fine enough for younger kids, but the design and lack of games feel more like an “older kids’ watch” to me, and my 12-year-old son agrees. Either way you go, these are fantastic choices that you’ll be happy with, especially with a nice little deal.

#1805. Industry News: Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA notes nearby phones will be jammed too.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA notes nearby phones will be jammed too.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1293 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons.
  • Industry observers note that wireless industry lobby group CTIA mentioned a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls.
  • Recent findings suggest that the pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons.

Industry observers note that wireless industry lobby group CTIA mentioned a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls. CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing:.

Recent findings suggest that the pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate. Even with these constraints, the micro-jamming system blocked 911 calls, interfered with public safety and other communications, and caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away. At the same time, the pilot results show substantial gaps in jamming the targeted “contraband” devices, with testing scenarios in outdoor inmate recreation areas showing failure rates—meaning “contraband” device call completion—in one-half to two-thirds of call attempts.

CTIA stated the pilot test indicates “that current jamming technology seems to be both over and underinclusive at once—it risks blocking lawful communications even as it fails to block a significant portion of the targeted contraband device communications.”.

The FCC approved the jamming order at its meeting yesterday. “Today, we are finally authorizing state and local prisons and jails to use targeted jamming against contraband cell phones for the first time,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said. “The technology has advanced to the point where it can be focused with geographic precision. No facility will be required to do it.”.

The Communications Act prohibits willful or malicious interference with licensed or authorized radio communications, and the FCC has previously interpreted this to prohibit non-federal entities from using jamming technology on contraband devices at prisons. Yesterday’s vote provides an exception for state and local correctional facilities. The FCC claims its jammer prohibitions do not apply to federal agencies because the federal government’s use of spectrum is not regulated by the agency.

Carr said that “contraband cell phones continue to pour into prisons by the thousands each year,” with “estimates indicat[ing] that as many as 500,000 inmates nationwide have regular access to these devices.” He said the phones have been used to plan scams, drug trafficking, and violent attacks.

“In Georgia, an incarcerated gang leader directed a drive-by shooting that killed two 13-year-old boys at a birthday party,” Carr said, referring to a 2024 shooting.

Carr defended the strategy against criticism that it will block legitimate communications outside the prisons, saying it includes safeguards to prevent that.

It has been revealed that “Those that want to use the technology will apply to the FCC, explain how they blueprint to deploy it, and show through testing that it stays inside the designated area and doesn’t interfere with lawful communications outside the prison walls,” Carr said. “Communities nearby will receive notice before operations start. We’re also seeking comment on next steps, including ways to close remaining loopholes on other frequencies and the possibility of quiet zones around correctional facilities.”.

Freedom of the Press Foundation Chief of Advocacy Seth Stern stated the FCC should have considered the benefits of contraband phones being used to document abuses inside prisons.

Sources indicate that “Prisons are the most secretive government institutions in the country and people wishing to expose abuses and inhumane conditions from the inside often do not have many options,” Stern wrote in a letter to FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez’s office, which was included on the FCC docket. “Last year’s Oscar-nominated film, The Alabama Solution, used footage incarcerated people captured with contraband cell phones to show Americans some of the awful things that go on in state prisons that they’d have no other way of seeing. The same footage bolstered an ongoing DOJ investigation into Alabama prisons and was crucial evidence in a civil lawsuit by Steven Davis, who was brutally killed by prison guards, that eventually settled.”.

Jamming contraband cellphones was supported by prison phone companies ViaPath (aka Global Tel*Link) and NCIC Correctional Services, the National District Attorneys Association, the Correctional Leaders Association, and National Association of Police Organizations.

“Inmates have used these phones to coordinate attacks against correctional officers and their families, as well as inmate violence, strikes, disturbances, and full-scale riots,” the National Association of Police Organizations said. “They also use contraband phones to organize deliveries of illegal drugs and weapons into correctional facilities. These dangers underscore the need to authorize indoor jamming in state and local correctional facilities.”.

Gomez, the only Democrat on the three-member commission, said she’s concerned about potential unintended consequences, but voted with Republicans to allow jamming after safeguards were added to the order.

Sources indicate that “For the last 90 years, the Federal Communications Commission has prohibited jamming by non-federal actors and even prohibited jamming equipment to be introduced into the American market,” Gomez noted. “That is because jamming devices are specifically designed to interfere with communications devices in order to render them un-usable.”.

Gomez noted that “jamming can prevent devices from completing 911 and emergency calls as well as interfere with communications networks used by fire, police, Emergency Medical Services, and other public safety entities.” She also said making jamming equipment available in the American market could lead to “unauthorized sale of this hazardous equipment,” and that “the accessibility of jamming equipment can itself motivate criminal enterprise.” Criminals have used “Wi-Fi jammers to disrupt security systems, security cameras, and cellphones to conduct robberies at homes and at stores,” she said.

Gomez said she’s glad the final order includes safeguards “to ensure that jamming is contained to this unique use, to permit jamming by a very limited category of authorized actors, and to take as much care as possible to prevent jamming and jamming equipment from becoming a hazard to safety.”.

Recent findings suggest that gomez partially dissented because she is worried the FCC will let correctional facilities and prison phone companies charge higher prices for inmate calling services that connect inmates with family members. Under US law, the FCC sets limits on those prices and considers prisons’ and jails’ safety and security costs when deciding how much money they can charge, she noted.

Sources indicate that gomez remarked, “While correctional facilities should have safety and security services like jamming to prevent criminal activity, it is not the responsibility of the families of incarcerated people to pay for the costs of these measures… Jamming is specifically designed to block communications and is certainly not necessary to provide phone and video calls for incarcerated individuals. We should have made this clear in today’s order. Because we failed to do so, I dissent in part.”.

The FCC order could be challenged in court. The CTIA has argued that the FCC “has no authority to allow jamming” under the Communications Act, which directs the FCC to prevent interference.

According to recent reports, AT&T said the FCC’s legal justification “is premised on a fundamental factual error: the assumption that jammers will only block ‘unauthorized’ communications without impacting lawful uses. There is no way to jam some communications on a spectrum band but not others. That is because radio jammers ‘block all wireless communications on affected spectrum bands,’ and, as the FCC has noted in the past, ‘cannot differentiate between contraband devices and legitimate devices.’”.

It has been revealed that AT&T said that “there is simply no way to limit the reach of jammers to the confines of a given facility. Jammers have been shown to cause interference outside the facilities in which they operate, greatly increasing the risk that someone living or traveling nearby will be impacted.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The price of the bitcoin dropped 22.7% in the 30 days before Anthropic's IPO and fell 22.3% in the month leading up to SpaceX's June 12 listing.
  • In a recent development, "Liquidity events can elevate correlations across asset classes quickly," Matthew Sheffield, chief investment officer at the ether treasury firm Sharplink, told CNBC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin has suffered nearly identical sell-offs ahead of two of the biggest public offerings this year, leaving investors wondering if competing demand for investor capital could be weighing on the cryptocurrency and perhaps delaying its recovery.

The price of the bitcoin dropped 22.7% in the 30 days before Anthropic's IPO and fell 22.3% in the month leading up to SpaceX's June 12 listing. Ether declined 25.3% in the 30 days preceding Anthropic's debut, and 28% in the same window ahead of SpaceX.

In a recent development, "Liquidity events can elevate correlations across asset classes quickly," Matthew Sheffield, chief investment officer at the ether treasury firm Sharplink, told CNBC. "The first 15 min of [Thursday's] Anthropic IPO put that on full display. Tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, crypto all sold off as traders sold assets to buy shares in the secondary market.".

"Stores of value function as such over long horizons, but in the short term are still liquidity driven," Sheffield stated. "We saw this in early Covid when the market fled to cash. Stock, bonds, commodities ... it didn't matter, you were being sold for cash.".

Sources indicate that while investors appear to be rotating capital out of crypto to make room for history-making IPO investments, that can't be remarked with precise certainty. Crypto has also been under pressure from ETF outflows, leverage, macro uncertainty and broader risk-off sentiment.

In a recent development, still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next. With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns.

It has been revealed that "[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," remarked Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management, a bitcoin treasury firm. "My view is that [for] bitcoin, the most likely scenario is that it chops around here.".

The expiration of IPO allocation restrictions can influence the timing of capital flows into digital assets, Sheffield mentioned.

"Post SpaceX we saw the wealth effect in full force," Sheffield mentioned. "Many brokers make traders wait 15-30 days before they are allowed to flip shares they received as allocations. … If you went long ETH versus SpaceX on the day of the IPO, on day 31 was when you would have become profitable.".

It has been revealed that bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen. On Friday, it was sitting at about $62,000.

As of Friday, bitcoin was hovering at the upper end of a critical $60,000 to $62,000 support range. Its next move could determine whether it can stabilize or if it will face another leg lower and revisit its July low of $57,737.35.

Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand.

Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole. Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he noted.

"Capital markets are open, … retail fears are high, and when you combine those things it's much more likely to be a dip-buying opportunity across the board, including bitcoin, than the start of a great financial crisis," stated Cole. "It'll likely age as a volatile time to consider allocating to risk, not the opposite.".

"The winter for bitcoin is basically at the end, but after winter does not come summer, it comes early spring," he added. "Anytime anyone's been around early spring, what you notice is it gets really cold still, it still rains – it's not necessarily great weather, and I think that's the environment we're in for bitcoin.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.

An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how rapidly AI is transforming mathematics.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

In a recent development, anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.

Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website, Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the firm’s IPO on Thursday.

Recent findings suggest that the Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most crucial unsolved problems in mathematics.

A statement on Alpöge’s website indicates Claude was integral to developing the proof:.

I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.

The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic mentioned it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August, but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”.

It has been revealed that alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules, a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”.

Sources indicate that in the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture, a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.

It has been revealed that openAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.

OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar.

Recent findings suggest that though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge mentioned in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sony’s iconic Walkman headphones are back in the USB-C MDR-3R and, after swiftly selling out on launch day, they’ve now been restocked. And, after using them, I can see why they sold out so quickly.

Sources indicate that the MDR-3R are Sony’s revival of the wired over-ear headphones that many used with a classic Walkman player. The retro style still looks great in 2026, but using an original pair is a bit of a headache in today’s age of headphone jack-less smartphones. So it was nice to see Sony give this a revival with USB-C.

And, yeah, they live up to the hype.

While the style won’t be for everyone, I think these work brilliantly. The sound quality is excellent and having a pair of headphones that doesn’t fully enclose my ears is pretty refreshing. There’s no noise cancellation, but with open-ear earbuds becoming more popular, I actually really like these as a similar solution (though high volumes will definitely be heard by those around you). I’m not fully cut off from the world around me, but I’m also able to get good sound quality. Lows are the weakness here, with unimpressive bass drops, but the sound quality is crisp and clear and pretty neutral, and the open-ish style makes it feel like the room around me is filled with music.

The physical hardware is great. While a plastic and metal build is objectively not as comfy as a premium pair of ANC headphones, the extremely light weight helps MDR-3R become an afterthought. You simply forget you’re wearing them after a few minutes.

The earpads are swappable, with orange and blue options included in the box.

Sources indicate that as for the USB-C cable, it’s fully plug-and-play. No app needed and it worked across every device I tested (including Pixel, which doesn’t work with all USB-C audio output). I do wish the cable was perhaps a few inches longer, but it’s long enough to wear the headphones with my phone in my front pocket. There’s a remote along the cable for play/pause and volume adjustments, though I think it’s a little too high on the cable.

For $59.99, these are a fun pair of USB-C headphones to have on hand. They sound good, work great, and don’t cost an arm and a leg. I can see why they sold out so quickly on launch day – in just 10 hours, Sony told me.

According to recent reports, sony MDR-3R are back in stock now and shipping in early December. If you want a pair, I say don’t wait. They’re well worth at least trying if you can get them for retail price – please don’t give in to the scalpers selling these at double, they’re not worth that.

Grand Theft Auto VI has quite a stacked soundtrack.

Cardi B, Travis Scott, Dua Lipa, Justice, Lana Del Rey — these are just some of the artists whose music can be heard on dozens of in-game radio stations.

GTA 6's plethora of licensed music has led to some viral moments, like the clip of streamer caseoh rocking out to Ariana Grande in real life while chilling out in a car in the game.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Industry observers note that thankfully, Rockstar Games has kept streamers and content creators in mind and gave them an easy way to shut off licensed music. Here's how to do it.

Simply pause the game by pressing the option or menu button on your controller.

Next, scroll down to the Settings option.

In the Settings menu, head to the very last tab labeled Audio.

Finally, scroll down to Mute Licensed Music and toggle this option on.

This option will mute all the licensed music in the game and ensure your streams and videos don't get taken down.

Industry observers note that there are some things to note. Rockstar Games does not provide any royalty-free replacement music. If a licensed song is playing on the radio in-game, users won't hear anything until a radio show host or original song comes on. With that noted, original music created for the game will continue to play. In addition, captions for licensed music will still appear on screen even though the music won't be audible.

According to recent reports, you can always roll the dice and hope a song played on the radio in GTA 6 doesn't take down your stream or clip. But, this Mute Licensed Music option will help you avoid any potential complications.
